planting.note: Set out container divisions in spring in lean, well-drained soil in full sun; this true dwarf holds a tight, low mound rather than sprawling like its taller relatives.

directions: Little Titch is one of the smallest catmint selections in cultivation, forming a dense, low hummock of tiny gray-green leaves topped with short spikes of lavender-blue flowers in late spring. Its diminutive scale makes it ideal for rock gardens, trough plantings, and the very front edge of a border where larger catmints would overwhelm neighboring plants. Give it gritty, fast-draining soil and full sun; in heavy or overly rich ground it loses its compact habit and becomes loose and floppy. Shear lightly after the first bloom flush to tidy the mound and coax a smaller repeat bloom later in summer. Essentially pest-free, deer- and rabbit-resistant, and a reliable draw for bees.

planting.note: Divide and transplant in spring into lean, well-drained soil in full sun; the white flowers show best against the plant's soft gray-green foliage in cooler weather.

directions: Snowflake is a rare white-flowered sport of dwarf catmint, offering the same low, spreading mound of aromatic gray-green foliage as the species but with clean white blooms instead of the usual lavender-blue, making it a useful accent for moon gardens or pale-toned borders. It shares the species' strong preference for lean, sharply drained soil in full sun and its tolerance of heat and drought once established. Deadhead or shear after the first bloom cycle to encourage a lighter secondary flush and keep the mound neat. Like other dwarf catmints it is generally untroubled by deer, rabbits, or serious pests, and bees visit the flowers readily despite their paler color.

planting.note: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost and press seed onto the surface, as it needs light to germinate; foliage color develops best with some afternoon shade in hot climates.

directions: Golden Feverfew is grown as much for its chartreuse-to-gold, finely cut foliage as for its small daisy-like flowers, making it a popular edging and container plant in addition to a medicinal herb. The bright leaf color is most vivid in cool spring weather and with light afternoon shade; intense summer sun can bleach or scorch the foliage in hotter regions. Shear plants back hard after the main bloom flush to refresh the color and habit, and remove spent flowerheads to reduce volunteer seedlings, since this form can revert toward green foliage from self-sown seed. As with the species, harvest the aromatic leaves fresh for tea or tincture, and handle with gloves since the foliage can irritate sensitive skin.

planting.note: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost, pressing seed onto the soil surface without covering; the fully double blooms make this selection popular for cutting.

directions: White Wonder produces fully double, all-white pompom flowers rather than the single daisy blooms of the species, giving it a look closer to a miniature chrysanthemum and making it a favorite for cutting gardens and dried arrangements. Culturally it behaves like the species: it tolerates poor soil and drought once established but flowers best with regular moisture and a sunny spot. Deadhead spent blooms frequently to extend flowering and to prevent the plant from setting seed, since double-flowered selections often produce a mix of double and single offspring when they self-sow. Cut stems for indoor arrangements just as the pompoms fully open, and divide or replace clumps every few years as vigor declines.

common_name: Golden Ball Feverfew (Double Yellow Button Feverfew)

planting.note: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost and surface-sow, as seed needs light to germinate; the tidy button-form flowers hold their shape well for drying.

directions: Golden Ball is a compact, dwarf feverfew selection bearing small, fully double, golden-yellow button flowers with no visible ray petals, quite distinct from the typical white daisy of the species. Its short, tidy habit suits front-of-border plantings and pots better than the taller straight species. Grow it in average, well-drained soil in full sun with even moisture for the heaviest bloom; established plants tolerate short dry spells but flower less freely under stress. Shear back after the first flush to encourage rebloom and remove spent flowerheads regularly to keep the compact form from becoming leggy. The button flowers dry well for everlasting arrangements while still being usable medicinally like other feverfew forms.

planting.note: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost, pressing seed onto the surface for light-dependent germination; a reliable heirloom double-flowered strain for cottage gardens.

directions: Ball's Double White is an old heirloom feverfew strain prized for its abundant, fully double, snowball-like white flowers held above finely divided, aromatic foliage on stems somewhat taller than most modern dwarf selections. It performs best in average to fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, and benefits from consistent moisture during bud formation for the fullest blooms. Pinch young plants once to encourage branching, and deadhead spent flowers continually through summer to prolong bloom and limit self-seeding, since seedlings often revert to single flowers. Like the species, the foliage is the medicinal part of the plant and can be harvested fresh for tea or tincture, though gloves are recommended when handling large quantities.
